title: Give each identity just enough access
lead: Start with who is acting, which resource is involved, and which operation is necessary.

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.body: IAM binds principals to roles on resources. A service account is an identity for a workload. Separate production from development and assign human permissions through groups so membership changes remain manageable.

sections.title: Make the decision
sections.body: Grant the narrowest useful role at an appropriate resource scope. Prefer attached workload identities or impersonation over downloading long-lived keys. Network restrictions do not replace identity permissions.

sections.title: Work through a scenario
sections.body: A nightly loader reads one bucket and writes one dataset. Give its service account those permissions; the engineer running it does not need to remain Project Owner.

sections.title: Separate four identities
sections.body: Identify the human or automation submitting a job, the workload identity reading the data, the service agent managing infrastructure, and the downstream consumer. They can require different grants. A service account is not a collection of credentials: it is the principal. A key is only one way to authenticate as that principal.

sections.title: Follow the permission through the hierarchy
sections.body: A narrowly scoped local grant does not erase a broader inherited grant. Inspect organization, folder and project access before concluding that production is isolated. Granting a group access makes membership easier to manage, but the group itself must still be governed. Audit both role bindings and who can alter membership.

sections.title: Prefer short-lived credentials where possible
sections.body: For an external CI workload, federation can exchange a trusted external identity for short-lived Google credentials. For a workload already running on Google Cloud, an attached identity is often the simpler starting point. Impersonation permission is itself powerful; granting it broadly can defeat otherwise narrow data permissions.

trap: A project-wide Editor role creates more exposure than a bucket reader and dataset writer need.

exercise.prompt: A job submitter has permission to start Dataflow, but workers cannot read a bucket. Which permission chain should you inspect?
exercise.answer: Inspect the worker service account actually attached to the job and its effective bucket permissions. Also verify that the submitter may use that identity. Giving the human more project-wide permissions is not evidence that the worker gained read access.
checkpoints: Name the principal that accesses each resource.
Distinguish inherited access from a local binding.
Explain why a downloaded key is not an IAM role.

briefing.context: A scheduled loader needs one bucket and one dataset. It should not be able to change every resource in the company.
briefing.whyItMatters: If the job is misused, its permissions determine how much data can be exposed or changed.

title: Trace identities across a private pipeline
lead: Find the real principal and network path at every boundary.

sections.title: Build an identity map
sections.body: List the person or CI process submitting work, the service agent creating resources, the worker account and the identities of downstream readers. For each operation, write principal, action and resource. This prevents a common diagnostic mistake: changing the submitter’s role when a worker is failing to read data.

sections.title: Then build a network map
sections.body: For each endpoint, verify resolution, route, firewall controls and the service’s supported private-access configuration. Reaching an API is not the same as being authorized to use it. A Shared VPC introduces host-project subnet administration as well as service-project job administration.

sections.title: Use minimal evidence to narrow the fault
sections.body: Identify whether the error is an authorization denial, name-resolution failure, connection refusal or timeout. Follow the actual worker configuration rather than assuming a default identity. Use short-lived authentication mechanisms when appropriate and keep secrets out of code, logs and notebooks.

trap: Broad Project Owner grants can hide the boundary you need to understand.

exercise.prompt: The job launches, source reads succeed and BigQuery writes fail with an access error. Which boundary is the first focus?
exercise.answer: Inspect the sink write permissions of the identity performing the write, together with the dataset and job configuration. Starting the job and reading its source already provide evidence about other boundaries.
checkpoints: Map a principal to each operation.
Separate authorization from connectivity.
Keep credentials out of diagnostic output.

briefing.whyItMatters: Giving the engineer more access can leave the actual worker failure unresolved.

title: Protect the values, the keys and the boundary
lead: Encryption, authorization and data minimization solve different parts of the problem.

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.body: CMEK gives your organization control over encryption keys; it does not make every user authorized. Sensitive Data Protection can inspect and transform private values before analysts receive them.

sections.title: Make the decision
sections.body: Use row policies for allowed records and column policies for restricted fields. Use a service perimeter to reduce exfiltration across supported APIs. Check residency requirements for both processing and storage.

sections.title: Work through a scenario
sections.body: Support agents need active customers, while analysts need all customers without national IDs. Combine a row filter for support with protected or transformed sensitive columns for analysts.

sections.title: Choose the control by what must change
sections.body: Row policies restrict records. Column policies restrict fields. Masking changes which representation a permitted reader receives. De-identification transforms the data itself. An authorized view exposes a chosen query result. Encryption protects data under a key-management model; it does not decide which business rows an analyst should see. Combine controls when the requirement spans these layers.

sections.title: Keep permissions separate from geography
sections.body: Selecting a dataset location and constraining resource creation address different concerns. Also inspect where processing, staging, exports and recovery copies occur. A regional label is not proof of compliance with every legal requirement, and a service perimeter is not a substitute for the dataset’s actual location.

sections.title: Trace key ownership and recovery
sections.body: For CMEK, the service performing the encryption must be allowed to use the relevant key and the supported key location must fit the service. Plan key access and recovery with the data recovery plan. Deleting a shared key can affect more records than intended; per-person cryptographic deletion requires deliberate key granularity.

trap: A firewall rule alone cannot express which BigQuery columns a user can read.

exercise.prompt: Analysts need all orders with masked identifiers; fraud investigators need original identifiers only for their cases. What must your design distinguish?
exercise.answer: Distinguish the allowed rows, column or masked-value access, and the identity of each reader. Define which users may obtain original values and check inherited grants. A single project role or bucket encryption setting cannot express all these business conditions.
checkpoints: Match a record restriction to row security.
Explain masking versus changing the stored dataset.
Include staging and backups in a residency decision.

briefing.whyItMatters: Access rules, encryption and privacy transformations protect different parts of the same data journey.
briefing.takeaway: Identify the value, identity and access boundary before choosing a security control.

title: Choose locations against residency and recovery
lead: A geographic requirement needs an explicit map of data copies and operations.

sections.title: List every place the data exists
sections.body: Include source capture, staging files, processing workers, warehouse datasets, temporary outputs, diagnostic logs and recovery copies. Ask whether the requirement covers storage, processing or both. Do not assume a single regional dataset setting constrains every other service in the route.

sections.title: Compare allowed geography with failure domains
sections.body: A rule restricting all copies to one region can conflict with a request to recover from that region’s complete loss. Surface that constraint explicitly and compare supported designs. A multi-region label should not be treated as a guarantee of any chosen failover behavior or zero recovery time.

sections.title: Validate access in the recovery environment
sections.body: The destination needs usable keys, roles, quotas, dependencies and a procedure to redirect consumers. Test with a controlled recovery copy and compare recovered business totals. Document which failure model, loss objective and restoration objective the evidence actually supports.

trap: Location, jurisdiction, availability and backup retention are related but different requirements.

exercise.prompt: A policy allows only one region, while the requested disaster plan requires another region. What is the right design response?
exercise.answer: Expose the conflicting constraints and obtain an approved recovery scope; do not quietly place a forbidden copy elsewhere or pretend a same-region copy satisfies regional loss.
checkpoints: Inventory staging and recovery copies.
Distinguish allowed geography from availability.
Test recovery permissions as well as data.

title: Make correctness part of the architecture
lead: A pipeline that finishes can still deliver the wrong result.

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.body: Define a data contract: required fields, valid ranges, unique identifiers and freshness. An idempotent operation has the same effect when retried with the same input. ACID transactions keep related database changes consistent.

sections.title: Make the decision
sections.body: Check counts and business totals as well as schema. Quarantine malformed records with an error reason. Test a representative fixed dataset before changing a production transformation.

sections.title: Work through a scenario
sections.body: A payment retry arrives twice. Store a stable event ID and make the write idempotent, then reconcile the final totals. Exactly-once processing alone does not protect an arbitrary external API call.

sections.title: Define the grain and the invariants
sections.body: The grain describes what one row represents: an order, an order line or an event observation. Define a stable business key at that grain. Quality rules should then protect required values, uniqueness, valid ranges and relationships. Reconcile a financial total as well as row counts: equal counts can still hide duplicated or corrupted values.

sections.title: Separate transport, processing and business effects
sections.body: At-least-once delivery can repeat a message. A processing engine may deduplicate its managed output while still retrying user code. A destination can support idempotent writes without making an unrelated API call transactional. State the guarantee at each boundary rather than describing the whole business flow with one exactly-once label.

sections.title: Make replay safe before you need it
sections.body: A stable event ID recognizes repeats; an ordering or version rule decides which update is newest. Keep the raw evidence and a reason for rejected records. Decide whether a replay replaces a partition, merges by key, or appends an explicitly versioned observation. Blindly appending rerun output can double the result.

trap: Do not equate an acknowledged message with a completed external business transaction.

exercise.prompt: A report has the correct row count but twice the revenue. What two checks would you add?
exercise.answer: Check the grain and join cardinality, then reconcile business totals against the source. A one-to-many join can multiply order-level revenue without changing an unrelated count metric. Use stable keys and test reruns against the same expected total.
checkpoints: State the grain before designing a key.
Name the exact boundary of a delivery guarantee.
Define what a replay should change.

briefing.whyItMatters: A successful pipeline can publish the wrong business total if it counts repeated events.

title: Design for the next requirement
lead: Keep data discoverable and make deliberate tradeoffs about portability.

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.body: Separate durable data from temporary compute. Open formats can make the same objects usable by multiple processing engines. A catalog records business meaning and technical metadata; lineage explains where an output came from.

sections.title: Make the decision
sections.body: Choose formats, regions and interfaces against actual business constraints. A portable file format does not automatically make permissions, orchestration or application code portable.

sections.title: Work through a scenario
sections.body: A team reuses data in Spark and a warehouse. Keep a documented object-storage landing area and govern the assets centrally rather than copying an undocumented dataset for each tool.

sections.title: Portability has several layers
sections.body: A readable open file format helps different engines consume data, but it does not transfer IAM bindings, private connectivity, scheduling or SQL semantics. Separate the durable data contract from the execution environment. Record partition layout, schemas, schema changes and ownership so another engine can reproduce the interpretation.

sections.title: Keep discovery connected to governance
sections.body: A catalog can describe assets and lineage across a platform. It is not automatically the authority granting access to every underlying object. A useful product contract identifies the owner, business meaning, access path, expected freshness and quality checks. A discovered dataset can still be unusable if those details are absent.

sections.title: Choose a measured migration boundary
sections.body: Preserve an existing Spark application when the business needs a fast move with minimal changes. Rewriting everything as warehouse SQL may be a later optimization rather than a prerequisite. Conversely, retaining a persistent cluster solely for a small SQL transformation can add unnecessary operational work.

trap: The guide says Dataplex; current documentation also uses Knowledge Catalog. Learn the governance capability as well as the name.

exercise.prompt: A team says that exporting Parquet makes its entire platform portable. What is missing?
exercise.answer: The file format addresses data readability. The team must also account for schema evolution, authorization, catalogs, network paths, transformation semantics and orchestration. Portability is a set of tested contracts, not a property guaranteed by a filename extension.

title: Migrate with a validation and cutover plan
lead: Estimate transfer time before choosing the transfer mechanism.

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.body: Inventory source formats, change rates, network capacity, dependencies and acceptable downtime. A full load moves existing records; change data capture tracks later changes. Reconcile counts, checksums or business totals before cutover.

sections.title: Make the decision
sections.body: Use Datastream for supported database change capture, scheduled connectors for supported recurring imports, and Storage Transfer Service for object or file movement. Consider Transfer Appliance when offline movement suits the timeline.

sections.title: Work through a scenario
sections.body: At 20 megabits per second, 1 petabyte needs about 12.7 years of ideal continuous transfer. A six-month deadline requires a different path; protocol tuning cannot close that gap.

sections.title: Inventory before selecting a connector
sections.body: Record the source engine and version, formats, primary keys, change volume, update and delete behavior, network route and downtime limit. A named managed transfer product does not support every proprietary source. Database migration and warehouse ingestion are also different destination problems. Choose only after checking the supported source-to-target path.

sections.title: Separate the snapshot from later changes
sections.body: A bulk backfill moves the existing state. Change capture carries later modifications. Plan the transition so changes during the backfill are not lost or applied in the wrong order. Reconcile key counts and business values, and define how deletes are represented. Keep a rollback decision until validation is complete.

sections.title: Use units in a transfer estimate
sections.body: For a lower-bound estimate, transfer seconds = bytes × 8 ÷ bits per second. Convert units consistently and then allow for utilization, protocol overhead, competing traffic and retries. A link’s advertised capacity is not an end-to-end application guarantee. Offline appliances add shipping and handling time even if they reduce network transfer time.

trap: An unnamed proprietary file format is not automatically supported by a managed transfer connector.

exercise.prompt: A 10 TB snapshot is copied successfully while the source keeps changing. Is it safe to redirect production immediately?
exercise.answer: Not from that evidence alone. Verify change capture coverage, catch-up lag, updates and deletes, business reconciliation, consumer compatibility and a rollback condition. A completed bulk copy does not prove that the destination represents the current source state.

Calculate a transfer lower bound with explicit units.
Define validation and rollback criteria.

title: Move from a snapshot to a changing source
lead: Plan updates, deletes, ordering and cutover as one contract.

sections.title: Define initial and incremental state
sections.body: A snapshot is a representation of the source at a point or supported consistent boundary. CDC records later changes. The transition must cover modifications occurring during the full load. Check the connector’s supported source semantics rather than assuming event timestamps alone establish a consistent order.

sections.title: Design the destination interpretation
sections.body: An event history can append each observed change, while a current-state table needs a version-aware application rule. Handle deletes deliberately. If multiple source versions arrive, a stale update must not overwrite a newer one simply because it was processed last. Deduplicate competing source versions before a MERGE when necessary.

sections.title: Make cutover a measured decision
sections.body: Measure source-to-target lag and compare source and destination business invariants. Test consumer queries against the new schema. Define what would trigger rollback and how any writes during the switch are reconciled. A green bulk-load job is only one part of the decision.

trap: Source change order and processing arrival order are not interchangeable.

exercise.prompt: Version 4 for an entity arrives after version 5. What should a current-state merge do?
exercise.answer: Keep the newer accepted version under the chosen source ordering contract. A MERGE condition and pre-deduplicated source should prevent the stale update from overwriting it.

Describe update and delete behavior.
Define cutover and rollback evidence.

title: Match the migration tool to the movement contract
lead: Measure volume and available bandwidth, then separate object movement, offline shipping and database change capture.

sections.title: Choose by what moves
sections.body: Storage Transfer Service manages supported file and object transfers. Transfer Appliance provides a physical data shipment route into Cloud Storage. For an ad hoc copy, gcloud storage cp is a command-line option. None of these facts makes a file-copy tool a database log reader.

sections.title: Use a lower-bound estimate
sections.body: Illustrative planning model: 100 TB (decimal) over a sustained 1 Gbit/s link requires about 9.26 days before overhead: bytes × 8 / bits per second. Shared capacity, retries, validation and change traffic increase the required window. Compare that window with appliance shipping and upload logistics rather than assuming offline is always faster.

sections.title: Validate before switching readers
sections.body: For files, reconcile object counts, checksums where applicable, naming and access. For a changing database, choose a supported migration or CDC path and reconcile a consistent snapshot plus subsequent changes. Datastream and Database Migration Service have different destinations and use cases; validate the exact source/target pair.

trap: A copied snapshot does not include changes made after that snapshot.

exercise.prompt: A small one-time folder copy and a nightly on-premises file feed share a Cloud Storage destination. Must they use the same tool?
exercise.answer: No. Consider gcloud storage cp for the ad hoc copy and a supported scheduled Storage Transfer Service job for the recurring feed. Check access, source support, connectivity and validation in both cases.

title: Define the source, sink and network path
lead: Draw the complete route a record must travel.

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.body: A source emits records, transforms change them, and a sink stores or serves the result. Specify latency, throughput, schema and delivery behavior. Verify that workers can reach both data endpoints and required Google APIs.

sections.title: Make the decision
sections.body: Private workers need an appropriate subnet, API access and IAM permissions. In a Shared VPC, distinguish the worker identity, job submitter and Google-managed service agent.

sections.title: Work through a scenario
sections.body: Dataflow reads Kafka on premises and writes BigQuery. An existing private connection may let KafkaIO read directly, avoiding an extra message bridge and its latency.

sections.title: Write a contract for every boundary
sections.body: Describe the source schema, event identity, time semantics, maximum acceptable lag and destination behavior. Include what happens to bad records and who is responsible for fixing them. A pipeline can meet its worker CPU target while failing the business requirement because the final data is stale.

sections.title: Trace the complete private route
sections.body: A worker may need to reach a database, object storage, an API endpoint and an artifact or dependency repository. Check DNS, routes, firewall controls, subnet selection and Google API access for each path. IAM can permit an operation while networking still prevents the connection, and the reverse is also possible.

sections.title: Distinguish control and data planes
sections.body: Creating a job is a control-plane action; workers reading and writing records perform data-plane actions. With a Shared VPC, permission to submit a job in the service project does not alone establish subnet access in the host project. Follow the current service-specific identity guidance rather than granting broad administration to an arbitrary account.

trap: Granting Dataflow Admin does not by itself grant permission to use another project’s subnet.

exercise.prompt: A Dataflow job starts but cannot reach an on-premises database. What evidence should you collect first?
exercise.answer: Identify the actual workers, selected subnet, resolved destination, connection route and failure message. Check private connectivity and firewall policy alongside the worker identity’s database and cloud permissions. Starting the job proves control-plane access, not complete data-plane connectivity.

title: Separate Pub/Sub delivery, ordering and replay
lead: A messaging guarantee must be tied to its supported subscription and region.

sections.title: Delivery is not a unique business event
sections.body: A publisher retry can submit the same logical order as distinct messages. A supported exactly-once pull subscription addresses its documented delivery contract; it does not automatically recognize two different message IDs as the same business order. Preserve a stable business ID and protect external effects.

sections.title: Ordering has a key and a scope
sections.body: Supported ordering preserves related publication order under the configured ordering-key and regional requirements. It does not impose one event-time order across all keys or prove which globally distributed business event physically occurred first. Consider the impact of slow work for a key on later related messages.

sections.title: Replay depends on retained history
sections.body: A seek can replay retained input, but enabling retention after old data was discarded cannot recover that missing history. A snapshot records acknowledgement state under its documented lifetime. Before deploying risky subscriber changes, decide which retained history and safe output contract make rollback useful.

trap: Exactly-once delivery is not an automatic end-to-end payment transaction guarantee.

exercise.prompt: Two publishers send the same business order with different Pub/Sub message IDs. Is subscription exactly-once enough?
exercise.answer: No. It addresses the supported message delivery contract, not arbitrary publisher-level business duplication. The destination or business operation needs an idempotency contract using a stable business order ID.

title: Choose between Kafka compatibility and Pub/Sub delivery
lead: Start with existing clients, replay requirements and ownership of the event contract.

sections.title: Retain an ecosystem deliberately
sections.body: Managed Service for Apache Kafka runs managed Kafka clusters. Google provisions brokers from the configured compute resources, while the team still chooses topic retention. It is a candidate when Kafka clients, partitions and consumer groups are part of the application contract.

sections.title: Compare the contract
sections.body: Pub/Sub provides topics and subscriptions that decouple publishers from consumers. A Pub/Sub subscription is not a Kafka consumer group with identical behavior. Compare ordering scope, acknowledgment behavior, replay and authentication before choosing a migration path.

sections.title: Work through an original decision
sections.body: A team already operates a Kafka application and must preserve its client integration during a migration. Evaluate the managed Kafka service, then test network access and consumer recovery. A new application without that compatibility requirement can evaluate Pub/Sub without assuming broker semantics. Neither choice removes the need for durable business event IDs.

trap: Managed infrastructure does not make every duplicate business event disappear.

exercise.answer: The proposal must compare client compatibility, partition or ordering assumptions, replay behavior, identity, networking and recovery. Similar nouns are not an interoperability guarantee.

title: Choose the engine that fits the work
lead: Minimize necessary code changes, then consider operating effort.

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.body: Dataflow runs Apache Beam pipelines for bounded or unbounded data. Dataproc supports existing Spark and Hadoop ecosystems. Data Fusion provides visual integration. Dataform manages SQL transformations and dependencies in BigQuery.

sections.title: Make the decision
sections.body: Use existing workload compatibility as a constraint. A nightly SQL transformation does not automatically need a streaming engine; an existing Hive application may favor managed Spark/Hadoop tooling.

sections.title: Work through a scenario
sections.body: A team has hundreds of Spark jobs and a short migration deadline. Move durable inputs to Cloud Storage and keep the Spark execution model before planning a later SQL rewrite.

sections.title: Start with the existing execution model
sections.body: Beam and Dataflow suit a pipeline described as transforms over bounded or continuous collections. Spark and Hadoop compatibility can favor Dataproc or managed Spark. Dataform fits warehouse SQL graphs. Data Fusion offers visual integration. Workflows and Composer coordinate execution; they do not replace the engine doing every heavy transformation.

sections.title: Decide ETL versus ELT from the constraint
sections.body: ETL transforms before the analytical load; ELT loads a staging representation and transforms inside the warehouse. ELT can simplify a SQL-centric system, but it is not appropriate if unprotected sensitive values must never reach that staging location. Choose based on data handling, transformation needs, scale and ownership.

sections.title: Avoid choosing by a single adjective
sections.body: Serverless, managed and real time are not complete architectures. A service may reduce infrastructure work while still requiring schema design, identity configuration, dependency control and monitoring. Compare compatibility, transformation expressiveness, expected delay and operation cost using the same workload.

trap: A product being serverless does not mean its processing, storage and network use are free.

exercise.prompt: A daily BigQuery SQL aggregate and an existing Spark ML job must both run. Must they share the same engine?
exercise.answer: No. Keep the SQL transformation in a suitable warehouse workflow and preserve the Spark execution model where that fits the application. Coordinate their dependencies and validate the shared data contract. Using one engine everywhere is not a requirement unless the business explicitly imposes it.

title: Find the limit before adding Dataflow workers
lead: Use stage-level evidence to distinguish capacity from parallelism.

sections.title: Different bottlenecks need different changes
sections.body: A source or sink can throttle the pipeline, a hot key can concentrate aggregation, a fused stage can restrict redistribution, and worker code can exhaust memory. Increasing the maximum worker setting does not guarantee that any of these constraints disappears. Inspect stage behavior and backlog together.

sections.title: Understand why work is or is not splittable
sections.body: Elements may be processed in parallel, but a particular grouping or stateful key can create a serial boundary. An explicit redistribution can help some fusion cases while adding materialization and network overhead. A hot-key redesign must preserve the aggregation semantics; random salting alone does not explain how results are recombined.

sections.title: Evaluate autoscaling with the full contract
sections.body: Check configured limits, available quota, job options, processing backlog and source/sink behavior. Compare a representative run before and after a change. Track output correctness and freshness, not just the number of active workers.

trap: More workers are not proof of more useful parallel work.

exercise.answer: Investigate hot-key concentration and the serial aggregation boundary. Consider a correctness-preserving partial aggregation and recombination strategy, then measure the affected stage rather than merely raising the global worker limit.

title: Reason about event time and late data
lead: When an event happened and when a worker saw it can be different.

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.body: A fixed window groups timestamps into equal intervals. A sliding window can overlap. A session groups activity separated by a chosen inactivity gap. A watermark estimates event-time progress; it is not a guarantee that every earlier event arrived.

sections.title: Make the decision
sections.body: Choose allowed lateness and triggers based on the tradeoff between early results and later corrections. Preserve source timestamps rather than replacing them with processing time.

sections.title: Work through a scenario
sections.body: A click created at minute 2 arrives after one created at minute 9. It belongs to the earlier event-time window, if that window is still allowed to accept data.

sections.title: Define what the output represents
sections.body: A fixed window has clock-aligned boundaries. A sliding window can include an event in overlapping intervals. A session merges activity according to an inactivity gap, typically after grouping by an entity key. Do not confuse an analytical SQL window function over table rows with a streaming event-time window.

sections.title: Separate watermark, trigger and retention
sections.body: The watermark estimates event-time progress. A trigger determines when a pane of results is emitted. Allowed lateness concerns how long a window may still accept delayed records. Source message retention concerns whether input can be replayed. These settings solve different problems and one does not replace the others.

sections.title: Design the downstream correction
sections.body: An early count may later change. Decide whether downstream consumers receive an updated aggregate, a replacement, or a sequence of panes they must combine correctly. Accumulating results can repeat earlier contributions; blindly summing every emitted pane can overcount. Test early, on-time and late arrivals with explicit expected totals.

trap: The first processed auction message is not necessarily the earliest bid.

exercise.prompt: A dashboard needs immediate provisional totals and corrected final totals. Is increasing allowed lateness enough?
exercise.answer: No. Specify a trigger and accumulation strategy for interim results, the lateness policy and a sink representation that handles corrections. Retention and replay are separate concerns. Validate the final total using a known sequence of delayed and repeated events.
checkpoints: Distinguish event time from processing time.
Explain what each window type groups.
Name how the sink applies a corrected aggregate.

briefing.whyItMatters: Using arrival time can put a valid event into the wrong reporting period.

title: Plan panes, late arrivals and corrected totals
lead: State when a result is emitted and what later updates mean.

sections.title: Assign the business timestamp
sections.body: Choose the event timestamp from the source contract. Events in a collection need keys and a windowing strategy suitable for their business aggregation. A record can arrive out of order without being invalid; dropping it changes the result and therefore requires a documented policy.

sections.title: Separate emission from completeness
sections.body: A trigger can emit an early pane before the watermark suggests expected completeness. Later panes can reflect additional records. Allowed lateness and state cleanup determine what remains possible after a window’s expected end. Exact details depend on the transform and runner configuration, so test the intended behavior.

sections.title: Match panes to a sink model
sections.body: If panes are cumulative, summing every pane as if each contained only new values double-counts earlier records. A sink may need keyed replacements or a documented accumulating representation. Use controlled delayed events to verify both the immediate dashboard and the final reconciled total.

trap: A watermark estimate is not an assertion that the network can never deliver an older event.

exercise.prompt: Cumulative panes contain counts 3 and then 5. What is the final count, and why not 8?
exercise.answer: The later cumulative pane already contains the earlier contributions, so the final count is 5. A downstream consumer must understand pane semantics rather than blindly add all emitted aggregates.

title: Route failures without losing the evidence
lead: A rejected record should remain explainable and recoverable.

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.body: Validate fields before loading typed warehouse tables. Separate valid rows from a dead-letter output containing the original payload, error type and event identifier. Distinguish permanent invalid data from temporary service errors.

sections.title: Make the decision
sections.body: Use bounded retry with backoff for transient failures. Monitor the failure output and define who repairs or replays it. A Pub/Sub dead-letter delivery-attempt limit is approximate rather than an exact retry counter.

sections.title: Work through a scenario
sections.body: An address column mixes formats. A visual Data Fusion transformation can standardize values, while a quarantine path keeps rows whose values cannot be interpreted safely.

sections.title: Separate data errors from service errors
sections.body: A missing mandatory key or malformed date usually needs correction of the record or transformation rule. A temporary API outage may benefit from bounded retry. Repeating permanent bad input indefinitely consumes capacity and blocks useful work without improving correctness. Classify the failure before selecting retry behavior.

sections.title: Keep a repairable error record
sections.body: An error output should preserve a stable identifier, the original or safely redacted payload, the validation rule, processing context and enough timing information to investigate. Protect this output as carefully as the primary dataset if it contains personal information. A dead-letter store is part of the data architecture, not a place where responsibility ends.

sections.title: Make reinsertion a controlled path
sections.body: Define how repaired records return to processing and how their identity prevents duplicate business results. Record the repair decision and monitor the growing backlog. A decreasing main-pipeline error rate can hide a worsening quarantine backlog if the two metrics are not considered together.

trap: Converting malformed CSV to Avro does not by itself repair the underlying values.

exercise.prompt: All invalid records are retained, but nobody reviews the error dataset. Is the data-quality problem solved?
exercise.answer: No. Retention preserves evidence but does not repair the business data. Assign ownership, measure the failure backlog, classify causes and define a safe replay path. Reconcile the repaired output with the expected business totals.

title: Choose load, stream and merge behavior explicitly
lead: Ingestion method determines visibility, retry and schema responsibilities.

sections.title: Batch loading and streaming solve different timing needs
sections.body: Recurring object files can fit a batch load or supported transfer configuration. A streaming writer serves a different freshness contract. Confirm the supported file format, compression, location and schema. A filename ending in JSON does not establish that a compressed file uses the newline-delimited structure the loader expects.

sections.title: Use offsets within their real boundary
sections.body: Correctly managed offsets on supported application-created Storage Write API streams can make repeated append attempts identifiable. The offset scope is a stream, not every message from every producer forever. Producer-side duplicate business events still require an appropriate identity and downstream interpretation.

sections.title: Make current-state updates deterministic
sections.body: For MERGE, define the match key and keep the source rows appropriate for the intended update semantics. Multiple source matches can produce errors for updating a target row. A deterministic latest-version selection is different from selecting an arbitrary row, especially when event times tie.

trap: The default write stream and offset-managed application streams do not have identical contracts.

exercise.prompt: A source batch has three updates for one target key. What should you define before MERGE?
exercise.answer: Define the source ordering and current-state selection, deduplicate to the intended row per key, and decide how older versions and deletes are handled. Do not assume MERGE invents the business rule.

title: Enrich records with models, carefully
lead: Model output is another data dependency with latency and quality constraints.

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.body: A Beam transform can validate records and route multiple outputs. Inference can add a predicted label. Generative enrichment also needs structured output validation, error handling and protection of sensitive inputs.

sections.title: Make the decision
sections.body: Batch requests where supported, control concurrency and test the chosen model adapter. Do not assume every text-generation endpoint can be called through any RunInference configuration without an integration.

sections.title: Work through a scenario
sections.body: For customer comments, validate the customer ID, remove unnecessary personal details, classify sentiment, and send malformed or failed inference results to review.

sections.title: Treat the model as a fallible dependency
sections.body: A successful HTTP call is not proof that the returned classification is valid. Check structured output, allowed labels, missing fields and service errors. Account for endpoint latency and request capacity when sizing a pipeline. Control concurrency so a temporary inference slowdown does not create an unbounded backlog.

sections.title: Control the input and the evidence
sections.body: Send only the information needed for the task. Separate untrusted document text from trusted processing instructions, retain the model and prompt version where permitted, and make results traceable to the input. Use human review where the application requires it rather than presenting generated values as validated ground truth.

sections.title: Choose where enrichment belongs
sections.body: In-pipeline inference can meet a before-load requirement but couples ingestion to model availability. A staged warehouse enrichment can simplify reprocessing when raw data is allowed in that environment. Select from the privacy boundary, latency target, supported model interface and recovery behavior instead of assuming a single product is always optimal.

trap: A confidently formatted model response can still be incorrect or fail your schema.

exercise.prompt: An enrichment endpoint returns an unknown label while the request status is successful. What should happen?
exercise.answer: Validate the response against the output contract and route or flag it for review. Preserve the input identity and error context for a controlled retry or repair. Do not silently invent a default business label merely to keep a success metric high.

title: Separate delivery from exactly-once processing
lead: State what is processed once, where duplicates can originate and what the sink promises.

sections.title: Choose a Dataflow processing mode
sections.body: Dataflow streaming uses exactly-once mode by default and also supports at-least-once mode. The latter can reduce cost and latency when duplicate processing is acceptable. Treat the decision as a correctness requirement before optimizing the execution mode.

sections.title: Trace the identifier
sections.body: Pub/Sub normally delivers at least once. Dataflow can deduplicate redeliveries, but an application can publish the same business event twice as distinct messages. Define a stable event ID rather than equating message identity with business identity.

sections.title: Inspect the final side effect
sections.body: Original scenario: a pipeline calls an external payment endpoint and then writes an analytical record. A processing guarantee is not proof that the endpoint cannot receive a repeated request. Design an idempotency contract at that endpoint and verify the sink write method separately.

trap: Exactly-once processing is not a blanket promise for arbitrary external side effects.

exercise.prompt: A repeated purchase is published with a new message ID. Is transport redelivery deduplication sufficient?
exercise.answer: No. Preserve a stable purchase identifier and make the business update idempotent. Verify pipeline and sink behavior independently.

title: Read the Beam model before choosing a runner
lead: The pipeline model describes data and transforms; a runner provides a particular execution environment.

sections.title: Distinguish the objects
sections.body: Apache Beam models a pipeline as transforms over collections. Bounded input can complete; unbounded input needs policies for grouping data over time. Dataflow is a managed execution service for Beam pipelines rather than a different name for the Beam SDK.

sections.title: Specify time behavior
sections.body: For an unbounded aggregation, define event timestamps, windows, triggers and allowed lateness. A window groups records; a trigger controls when results are emitted. A result emitted early may need correction when later data arrives.

sections.title: Port the contract, then test
sections.body: Original scenario: a team wants to reuse transformation logic across runners. Keep business logic separate from infrastructure settings and test connectors, supported features and sink semantics on the target runner. Model portability is useful evidence, but not a promise of identical performance or every connector behavior.

trap: A fixed window is not a timer that makes every event arrive on time.

exercise.prompt: An hourly event-time aggregation emits before all events arrive. Which separate policies must the design describe?
exercise.answer: Specify the event timestamp, window boundaries, trigger, lateness policy, accumulation behavior and how the sink represents corrections.

title: Evolve schemas without breaking consumers
lead: Treat the producer, transport, table and consumer as one versioned data contract.

sections.title: Check the allowed table operation
sections.body: BigQuery supports adding fields under documented mode and operation rules. Relaxing REQUIRED to NULLABLE differs from changing NULLABLE to REQUIRED, which requires a table recreation. Verify the supported change for the exact ingestion method and table type.

sections.title: Test both old and new records
sections.body: An optional field does not automatically have a safe business default. Original scenario: a new discount field is absent from old orders. Zero, unknown and not applicable represent different facts. Test old producers against new consumers and new producers against old consumers.

sections.title: Roll out with evidence
sections.body: Stage the new contract, replay representative historical records and inspect rejected rows. Keep a version identifier and a rollback plan. When a change alters meaning rather than representation, publish a new data product contract instead of silently rewriting history.

trap: Successful parsing is not proof that two schema versions mean the same thing.

exercise.prompt: A producer changes an optional amount field to mandatory. Will making the consumer table stricter repair old missing values?
exercise.answer: No. Backfill or explicitly reject the missing values under a documented rule, verify the table operation, and coordinate producer and consumer rollout.

title: Deploy a pipeline you can safely replace
lead: Make release behavior part of the design, before the first production run.

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.body: Version code and configuration, validate schemas, and test with representative records. A compatible streaming update can preserve state. An incompatible update needs a controlled replacement and recovery strategy.

sections.title: Make the decision
sections.body: Plan drain, source retention and replay together. Draining processes in-flight work; canceling may discard it. Decide whether the source can retain new messages while the replacement starts.

sections.title: Work through a scenario
sections.body: A windowing change is incompatible. Retain the source messages, drain the old job, start the replacement, and reconcile outputs rather than assuming a flag makes arbitrary state changes compatible.

sections.title: Version more than application code
sections.body: Record the schema contract, runtime dependencies, worker identity, network configuration and relevant job options with a release. A tested transform can still fail in production if the deployment changes a subnet or service account. Keep representative test inputs and output assertions with the release evidence.

sections.title: Choose the update path from compatibility
sections.body: A compatible stateful update and a replacement job have different requirements. Changes to state, coders or windowing can make an in-place update unsuitable. Review current upgrade guidance, source retention and the behavior of in-flight work before choosing drain or cancel. A deployment flag is not proof of semantic compatibility.

sections.title: Plan the reconciliation and rollback
sections.body: Define the expected output for the overlap or transition interval and how duplicates are recognized. Test a replay from retained source data in a controlled destination. Preserve a usable recovery path until you have evidence that the new release meets quality and freshness requirements.

trap: A successful CI deployment is not evidence that output totals remain correct.

exercise.prompt: Your integration tests pass, but the new job uses a different worker service account. What additional review is required?
exercise.answer: Review the effective permissions and private network path for that identity, along with artifact and source access. Then validate real output and freshness during a controlled release. Passing transformation tests does not prove that the deployed environment has the same access contract.

title: Gate publication on warehouse quality
lead: SQL as code should define both the table and its acceptance criteria.

sections.title: Separate validation from transformation
sections.body: A transformation creates a result; an assertion tests a property of it. Non-null, unique-key and row-condition checks can detect different failures. A custom assertion typically returns violating rows, with no violations representing success. Make business thresholds and required keys explicit rather than relying on a table creation success.

sections.title: Declare the gating dependency
sections.body: A downstream action may need to depend on upstream assertion results as well as the upstream table. Use the supported dependency configuration and test a failure path. An assertion appearing in the execution graph is not enough if the consumer can run before it passes.

sections.title: Design incremental runs and replay together
sections.body: An incremental filter selects what to process, while a merge or replacement rule defines what to write. Late corrections outside a short lookback can be missed. Decide how historical backfills and corrected source records reach the target, then compare rerun counts and business totals.

title: Start with the access pattern
lead: Select storage from the required reads and writes, not from dataset size alone.

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.body: BigQuery targets large analytical scans. Bigtable serves keyed, high-throughput access. Cloud SQL provides managed relational engines; Spanner supports strongly consistent distributed transactions. Cloud Storage stores objects. A cache such as Memorystore is a separate serving layer.

sections.title: Make the decision
sections.body: Ask whether the application needs joins, row lookups, multi-row transactions, document access or object reads. Firestore fits document-oriented applications; AlloyDB targets PostgreSQL-compatible relational workloads.

sections.title: Work through a scenario
sections.body: Sensor lookups need milliseconds while daily analytics need joins. Serve the keyed path from Bigtable and publish a warehouse copy for analytical scans.

sections.title: Ask six questions before choosing
sections.body: What does a read request look like? Which writes must be atomic together? How much data is read per request? What consistency is required? What availability and recovery scope are needed? Which engine or API compatibility must remain? Data volume alone cannot answer these questions. A one-row serving request and a terabyte scan can require different stores over related data.

sections.title: Separate a system of record from a serving projection
sections.body: A warehouse can retain analytical history while a keyed database serves low-latency application queries. A cache may accelerate derived values without replacing their durable source. Each additional copy needs an update contract, consistency expectation and recovery procedure; duplicating data is a design responsibility rather than a free optimization.

sections.title: Avoid overgeneralizing database labels
sections.body: NoSQL does not mean there are no transactions, and SQL does not mean every query pattern is efficient. Firestore supports a document model and transaction capabilities; Bigtable emphasizes keyed access; Spanner addresses distributed transactions. Check the actual transaction scope and access interface instead of deciding from the category name.

trap: A warehouse is not automatically the best transactional point-of-sale database.

exercise.prompt: A solution requires millisecond entity reads and daily cross-entity analytical joins. Why might two stores be reasonable?
exercise.answer: The access paths optimize different work. A keyed serving projection can handle individual entities while the warehouse handles scans and joins. The design must still explain how updates propagate, what lag consumers accept and how the projection is rebuilt.

title: Treat retention and cost as separate controls
lead: Cheap storage is useful only if its access and retention behavior fits.

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.body: Cloud Storage classes trade storage cost against retrieval and minimum-duration conditions. Lifecycle rules can change class or delete eligible objects. A retention policy prevents deletion until the required age; locking it is a consequential administrative choice.

sections.title: Make the decision
sections.body: Estimate the access pattern instead of assuming older data is never read. Distinguish availability, geographic placement, versioning and legal retention.

sections.title: Work through a scenario
sections.body: An audit archive is rarely read and must remain immutable for years. Choose an appropriate archival class and a retention policy, then test your retrieval procedure.

sections.title: Separate four independent decisions
sections.body: Bucket geography affects the placement and availability model. Storage class affects storage and retrieval economics. Lifecycle rules automate eligible object actions. Retention controls prevent premature modification or deletion under the configured policy. Choosing an archival class does not by itself make an object immutable or restrict who can read it.

sections.title: Model the actual access pattern
sections.body: Estimate how often data is read, how long it remains and how much is retrieved. A very cheap stored-byte rate can be offset by retrieval or minimum-duration conditions. Use current official pricing and class rules when deploying; a study scenario should identify the relevant cost dimensions rather than memorize a permanent dollar figure.

sections.title: Recoverability needs more than keeping old objects
sections.body: An organization can retain many versions but still lack the permissions, metadata or documented procedure needed to restore the intended state. Rehearse the recovery and confirm the required time and data-loss objectives. Consider how accidental deletions, overwrites and region failures differ.

trap: A lifecycle delete rule does not override an active retention requirement.

exercise.answer: A supported retention policy and any required lock or object protection must enforce the minimum period. IAM controls access separately. Storage class is an economic choice and does not replace retention enforcement or recovery testing.

title: Choose a database from the query and transaction
lead: Begin with access patterns, transaction boundaries, engine compatibility and recovery requirements.

sections.title: Separate analytical and operational reads
sections.body: BigQuery is designed for analytical work across records. Bigtable is a candidate for keyed high-throughput access when its row-key design fits the workload. Neither label alone proves the latency required by an application. Build a representative workload before choosing.

sections.title: State the relational requirement
sections.body: Cloud SQL offers managed familiar relational engines. AlloyDB is PostgreSQL-compatible. Spanner provides a distributed relational database with strong consistency. Compare supported features, transaction scope, scale and location requirements rather than choosing only from data size.

sections.title: Use multiple stores with explicit ownership
sections.body: Original scenario: checkout transactions and hourly historical sales analysis need different access paths. Keep an authoritative transaction system and publish validated analytical data. Document freshness, deletion propagation and reconciliation between the systems instead of demanding that one database serve every query.

trap: A cache hit rate is not evidence that the durable source can be recovered.

title: Model the warehouse around its queries
lead: Reduce repeated work without losing the meaning of a record.

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.body: Nested and repeated fields can represent related analytical entities without repeated joins. Partitioning separates data into segments; clustering organizes blocks within a table or partition. Column selection also affects scan volume.

sections.title: Make the decision
sections.body: Match partitions to common range filters and clustering order to selective access patterns. Preserve event identity and business keys. Avoid copying a transactional normalization rule into every analytical model.

sections.title: Work through a scenario
sections.body: Orders are queried by recent date and customer. Partition by order date, cluster by customer ID, and keep line items nested when that matches the reporting model.

sections.title: Model the business grain before optimizing
sections.body: An order-level amount should not be repeatedly summed after a join that expands one order into many lines. Define keys and cardinalities, then choose a model that represents the report’s grain. Nested and repeated fields can preserve a parent-child relationship without requiring the same join in every analytical query.

sections.title: Use filters that storage can exploit
sections.body: Partitioning helps when a query can eliminate partitions using an appropriate predicate. Clustering can skip irrelevant blocks within the remaining data. Column order matters for multi-column clustering. A selective-looking filter on an unrelated expression is not automatic evidence that the intended partitions or blocks were pruned. Inspect the actual plan and processed bytes.

sections.title: Keep changes and history explicit
sections.body: An append-only event table, a current-state dimension and a historical dimension answer different questions. Decide whether an update overwrites current truth or creates a new version. Use a stable key and a deterministic ordering rule for deduplication; a random choice among tied updates can make a rerun disagree with the previous output.

trap: LIMIT does not by itself reduce the bytes read from all referenced columns.

exercise.prompt: A report filters thirty days and a customer ID, but still scans much more than expected. What would you verify?
exercise.answer: Check the actual partition column and predicate, selected columns, clustering specification and query plan. Confirm the report is not expanding rows through joins or UNNEST. Compare measured processed bytes under the same input and filters before claiming a storage-layout improvement.
checkpoints: Explain the reporting grain.
Write a predicate that targets the partition.
Use a deterministic rule for current-state rows.

briefing.whyItMatters: Poor grain and layout can make results slower, more expensive or incorrect.
briefing.takeaway: Choose the business grain, then a layout aligned with the queries.

title: Read SQL at the grain of the business question
lead: Joins, arrays and analytical functions can change what one row means.

sections.title: Track cardinality through a query
sections.body: A one-to-many join repeats fields from the parent row. Summing a parent total after that expansion can multiply revenue. Pre-aggregate to a compatible grain or choose a representation that preserves the relationship. COUNT(DISTINCT parent_id) can fix one count but does not automatically fix every sum in the same query.

sections.title: Use analytical functions for a defined purpose
sections.body: ROW_NUMBER can select one observation per business key when paired with a deterministic ordering rule. A running total uses a partition, ordering and frame whose meaning should be explicit. QUALIFY filters analytical results; WHERE filters the relevant earlier row relation. None of these constructs chooses the correct business key for you.

sections.title: Handle unknown values and empty relationships
sections.body: NULL is not always zero: it may mean unavailable, inapplicable or unobserved. A WHERE filter on a nullable right-side column after a LEFT JOIN can remove rows without a match. When expanding arrays, verify how empty arrays affect the intended population and aggregation. Test these cases with tiny explicit fixtures.

trap: SUM(DISTINCT amount) is not a general repair for duplicated parent rows.
code:
WITH joined AS (
  SELECT 'o1' AS order_id, 100 AS order_total, 'a' AS item
  UNION ALL SELECT 'o1', 100, 'b'
  UNION ALL SELECT 'o2', 80, 'c'
)
SELECT SUM(order_total) AS wrong_grain_total
FROM joined; -- 280, not the order-grain total 180

exercise.prompt: Two orders total 100 and 80. The first has two items, the second one. What does SUM(order_total) after the item join return?
exercise.answer: The joined rows contain 100, 100 and 80, giving 280 instead of the intended order-grain total 180. Fix the grain or pre-aggregate; do not substitute a generally unsafe DISTINCT on the amount.
checkpoints: Predict row multiplication.
Explain a deterministic window ordering.
Preserve missing values and unmatched records deliberately.

briefing.takeaway: State what one row represents before joining and summing.

title: Make the lake usable, not just large
lead: Raw files need schema, metadata, access rules and quality checks.

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.body: A lake stores durable objects that different engines can process. Columnar formats can reduce work for analytical reads. BigLake can provide governed access to supported external data; a catalog makes assets discoverable.

sections.title: Make the decision
sections.body: Separate landing, validated and curated stages with explicit contracts. Monitor stale partitions and failed discovery. Check supported format and location combinations before choosing a query path.

sections.title: Work through a scenario
sections.body: A team needs reusable curated sales objects. Publish their schema, owner and freshness target, then validate incoming partitions instead of treating every uploaded object as trustworthy.

sections.title: Organize stages by their contract
sections.body: A raw landing area preserves received evidence; a validated layer enforces interpretable schema and basic quality; a curated product exposes business-ready meaning. The number of folders is not the important property. Each transition should say which validation was performed and whether a consumer may safely use its result.

sections.title: Choose access delegation deliberately
sections.body: A BigLake table can use a connection identity to reach supported external storage while readers receive table access. This differs from giving every analyst direct object permissions. The supported formats, locations, connector behavior and security features must fit the chosen source. A normal external table and a governed delegated-access design are not interchangeable labels.

sections.title: Monitor discovery and freshness separately
sections.body: Metadata discovery describes what exists; a freshness check asks whether the expected data arrived on time. A successful discovery scan can coexist with an incomplete daily partition. Monitor the input contract and data-quality result, not merely whether the catalog service is running.

trap: A catalog organizes metadata; it does not automatically cleanse every file it discovers.

exercise.prompt: New files are discoverable in the catalog but yesterday’s report is incomplete. Which contract should be examined?
exercise.answer: Inspect expected arrivals, partition completeness, transformation quality and report freshness. Discovery succeeded as a metadata operation; it did not prove that every business record or scheduled partition was present.
checkpoints: Explain what each lake stage guarantees.
Distinguish delegated table access from direct object access.
Separate discovery success from freshness.

briefing.whyItMatters: A large collection of files is hard to reuse without ownership, schema and quality evidence.
briefing.takeaway: Make the lake discoverable, governed and understandable to its readers.

title: Compare lake access with warehouse access
lead: Choose where the data stays and which identity reads it.

sections.title: Native and external storage imply different work
sections.body: A native warehouse table stores data in the warehouse service. An external table queries a supported external representation. Data movement, caching, format, location and performance needs influence the choice. Keeping files external is not automatically faster or cheaper for every frequently repeated analytical workload.

sections.title: Explain delegated access
sections.body: A BigLake connection can use a service identity to read supported underlying storage while consumer authorization is managed at the table layer. This can avoid broad direct object access for each analyst. The relevant connection and policy configuration still need explicit permissions and supported locations.

sections.title: Understand metadata and freshness
sections.body: File metadata caching can improve some external-query workloads, but cached metadata has refresh and supported-feature behavior. A recently changed object layout may not immediately be reflected by a cached view of the files. Choose a freshness contract and inspect the current feature limitations.

trap: An external table definition is not proof that every reader has the required governed access.

exercise.prompt: Analysts should query external files without receiving direct bucket access. What capability should you evaluate?
exercise.answer: Evaluate a supported BigLake delegated-access setup with a connection identity and table-level controls. Verify permissions, format and location. Do not simply grant every analyst object-viewer access and call it delegation.
checkpoints: Compare native and external access paths.
Name the identity reading the external objects.
Explain how metadata freshness affects a query.

briefing.whyItMatters: The table boundary is useful only if the selected access path actually enforces its policy.
briefing.takeaway: Trace the reader, connection identity and underlying storage separately.

title: Distinguish external BigLake access from managed Iceberg
lead: Identify who owns the files, who mutates the table and which access path enforces policy.

sections.title: Read the table type
sections.body: BigLake external tables delegate supported object-store access through a connection. Users can be granted table access without direct access to the underlying objects. Those external tables are read-only in BigQuery; do not generalize that limitation to every product containing BigLake or Iceberg in its name.

sections.title: Compare the managed format
sections.body: Apache Iceberg managed tables in BigQuery store data in customer-owned Cloud Storage buckets and support documented table mutations. BigQuery manages storage optimization and exports Iceberg metadata for interoperability. Check the current feature and limitation list for the exact table type.

sections.title: Apply the distinction
sections.body: Original scenario: a team wants governed read access over existing Parquet files. Compare an external BigLake table with loading a native table. A different team needs BigQuery-managed mutation of an open-format table in its own bucket; evaluate managed Iceberg and test its supported access paths.

trap: The words open format do not imply that every external engine may safely write the same managed table.

exercise.prompt: A design says all BigLake tables reject DML. What missing qualification should you request?
exercise.answer: Ask for the exact table type. BigLake external object tables and Apache Iceberg managed tables have different write contracts. Confirm the documented mutation path.
checkpoints: Identify the table type.
Separate file ownership from table management.
Verify the policy enforcement path.

decision.limitation: External-table and managed-table capabilities must be evaluated separately.
decision.useCase: Choose a lakehouse access model with explicit read and write ownership.

briefing.whyItMatters: External access and managed Iceberg tables have different mutation contracts.
briefing.takeaway: Ask for the exact table type and supported read and write paths.

title: Design lake files for the readers that use them
lead: A useful lake needs discoverable datasets, deliberate object layout and a lifecycle contract.

sections.title: Match layout to queries
sections.body: Columnar formats such as Parquet can be useful for analytical scans. Organize files around common filtering dimensions and test file-size distribution with the intended reader. Tiny files can add per-object overhead; one very large file can restrict parallelism depending on its format and reader. These are design hypotheses to measure, not universal size thresholds.

sections.title: Separate retention from retrieval cost
sections.body: Cloud Storage classes differ in storage and access economics. Lifecycle rules automate eligible object actions; retention controls protect required data. A cheap storage rate alone does not establish the cost of frequent access or early deletion.

sections.title: Make ownership visible
sections.body: Original scenario: a raw daily feed becomes a curated monthly data product. Keep the raw replay contract, curated schema, validation results and owner discoverable. Publishing metadata does not grant data access and cannot prove that the records are complete.

trap: Do not delete raw replay data merely because a curated table exists.

exercise.prompt: A lake is hard to query after millions of tiny daily files accumulate. Should the team change storage class first?
exercise.answer: First measure listing and scan overhead, reader parallelism and file layout. Consider a controlled compaction and catalog update while preserving replay and retention obligations; storage class addresses a different cost dimension.
checkpoints: Measure with the target reader.
Separate lifecycle and legal retention.
Keep ownership and quality evidence.

decision.advantage: A deliberate layout and catalog reduce discovery and query friction.
decision.limitation: Compaction and cleanup must preserve references, retention and replay guarantees.
decision.useCase: Publish queryable curated files while preserving controlled raw replay.

briefing.context: A query spends too much time opening millions of tiny lake files.
briefing.whyItMatters: A cheaper storage class does not automatically fix reader overhead or file layout.
briefing.takeaway: Measure the reader and preserve replay and retention during a layout change.

title: Give distributed teams shared guardrails
lead: Domain ownership can coexist with organization-wide standards.

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.body: Federated governance lets domain teams own data products while shared policies define discovery, quality, security and meaning. Catalog entries, lineage and business definitions reduce accidental misuse.

sections.title: Make the decision
sections.body: Identify an owner, approved access method, quality rules and a freshness expectation for each product. Use platform capabilities rather than building a separate spreadsheet catalog for each team.

sections.title: Work through a scenario
sections.body: Marketing and finance each publish curated assets. A shared catalog exposes their meaning and lineage, while storage IAM and table policies continue to control real access.

sections.title: Define a data product people can use
sections.body: A domain-owned asset needs an accountable owner, business definition, schema, access method, update expectation and quality evidence. Federated governance adds shared guardrails without making a central team perform every domain transformation. Publish enough context for consumers to understand what the product does and does not represent.

sections.title: Use lineage to investigate impact
sections.body: Technical lineage connects inputs, transformations and outputs. When a source changes, use it to identify potentially affected consumers; then review actual contracts and tests. A lineage edge alone does not establish that an output is correct, legally usable or fresh. Data quality and authorization remain separate evidence.

sections.title: Treat product names as time-sensitive
sections.body: The exam guide retains Dataplex and Dataplex Catalog terminology while current documentation can use Knowledge Catalog. Older notes may refer to Data Catalog APIs and role names. Preserve the architectural concept, but verify current migration and feature support before applying an old operational recipe.

trap: Governance metadata does not grant readers permission to the underlying data.

exercise.prompt: A new catalog automatically scans all tables. Does that implement federated governance?
exercise.answer: It provides part of discovery, but ownership, access policy, quality rules, lineage use and consumer contracts still need a deliberate design. Domain accountability and shared standards cannot be inferred from the mere presence of a catalog entry.
checkpoints: Describe ownership and consumer expectations.
Use lineage for a concrete change-impact question.
Check renamed or retired features against current docs.

briefing.whyItMatters: A catalog label alone cannot establish data quality or replace underlying permissions.
briefing.takeaway: Combine shared guardrails with accountable product ownership.

title: Make dashboards efficient and trustworthy
lead: Optimize the expensive operation that actually appears in the query plan.

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.body: Materialized views reuse supported computed results. BI Engine accelerates eligible analytical queries in memory. Partition filters and selective columns reduce scanning. Row and column access controls still apply to the data exposed to users.

sections.title: Make the decision
sections.body: Use execution details to locate expensive joins, skew or unnecessary scans. Check dashboard freshness and caching separately from warehouse ingestion freshness.

sections.title: Work through a scenario
sections.body: Hundreds of users repeatedly sum sales by day. A supported materialized aggregate avoids repeating the same large computation; BI Engine may further accelerate eligible dashboard queries.

sections.title: Inspect where the expensive work occurs
sections.body: A query can spend time reading unnecessary columns, shuffling a large join, processing a skewed key or sorting a large intermediate result. Start from the execution evidence and compare the same workload. More capacity may help resource pressure but does not make an avoidable row explosion a good query design.

sections.title: Choose the right reusable representation
sections.body: A logical view stores a query definition. A materialized view stores supported computed results and has specific refresh and query-shape rules. BI Engine accelerates eligible analytical work in memory. These mechanisms can complement one another, but none removes the need to understand filtering, freshness and authorization.

sections.title: Test end-to-end dashboard freshness
sections.body: Distinguish the time an event occurred, when it was loaded, when an aggregate was refreshed and when the dashboard cache was last updated. A freshly refreshed dashboard can still show stale upstream data. Define which timestamp the business freshness target refers to and monitor that interval.

trap: A logical view is a stored query definition, not automatically a stored result cache.

exercise.prompt: The dashboard refreshes every minute but shows hour-old values. Is adding slots the first justified action?
exercise.answer: No. Trace source arrival, ingestion completion, aggregate refresh and visualization caching. Use query execution evidence to decide whether compute is actually the bottleneck. Refresh frequency is not proof of end-to-end freshness.
checkpoints: Locate the expensive query stage.
Explain logical versus materialized views.
Trace freshness across the entire path.

title: Choose reusable results without losing freshness
lead: A fast dashboard should still answer the intended time-sensitive question.

sections.title: Compare the stored object
sections.body: A logical view stores a SQL definition. A materialized view stores supported computed results with refresh behavior and eligibility rules. A report cache stores a presentation-side response. They exist at different layers, so changing one does not automatically repair stale data in the others.

sections.title: Check the supported query pattern
sections.body: Incremental and non-incremental materialized-view options have different supported shapes and maintenance or freshness behavior. Inspect the current documentation rather than assuming every arbitrary SQL expression can be incrementally reused. Choose the simplest supported aggregate for a repeatable dashboard need.

sections.title: Measure end-to-end freshness and latency
sections.body: Record source event time, load time, aggregate refresh and dashboard read behavior. Compare the actual analytical query with and without the acceleration strategy while keeping authorization and business logic fixed. A lower query time and a fresh result must be demonstrated separately.

trap: Precomputation is not permission to ignore the business freshness target.

exercise.prompt: A logical view is fast on the second run. Does that prove it is a materialized view?
exercise.answer: No. A logical view remains a stored query definition; other caching can influence repeated execution. Inspect the actual object type and execution evidence before attributing a performance change.
checkpoints: Distinguish the three caching layers.
Check materialization eligibility.
Measure freshness separately from query latency.

briefing.whyItMatters: Reusing results can help, but a report still needs an explicit freshness contract.
briefing.takeaway: Compare reusable results against how much staleness the business permits.
